name: Eating clay (geophagy) and ice (pagophagia) in pregnancy
what_people_do: Some women, especially in the rural South, eat white or red clay, and some pregnant women eat large amounts of ice or freezer frost.
why_they_say_it_works: A cultural and family habit; women describe cravings and say it settles the stomach or helps the baby.

documented_by.source: Vermeer DE, Frate DA 1979, Am J Clin Nutr, PMID 484531
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Holmes County, Mississippi (Black population): geophagia in 57% of women and 16% of children, none among adult men; average 50 g of clay a day; 25 clay sources located.

documented_by.source: Edwards CH et al 1994, J Nutr, PMID 8201446
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Washington DC, 553 African American women in prenatal clinics: no geophagy observed; ice or freezer frost eating (pagophagia) in 8.1%.

evidence.tested: Clay eating and anaemia, hunger, worms, potassium
evidence.finding: Geophagia was not correlated with hunger, anaemia or helminths; may contribute to hypertension; did not support the hyperkalaemia idea.

source.name: Vermeer DE, Frate DA 1979, Am J Clin Nutr, PMID 484531

evidence.finding: Women with pica had lower serum ferritin and lower mean cell haemoglobin; infants had smaller head circumference.

source.name: Edwards CH et al 1994, J Nutr, PMID 8201446

harm_note: Pica is tied in these studies to lower iron stores in pregnancy; clay may raise blood pressure (Vermeer). Tell the midwife.
gaps: 1979 and 1994 data; current prevalence not found.
Clay content and contaminants not examined.
